title: Postcards and Language
premise: Cyrus Villalobos, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost his sense of taste after his mother's death, drifts through life writing about food he cannot feel. When a radio plays an unfinished song his late brother wrote and never recorded, Cyrus discovers the composer is alive — Marisol, the woman his family erased after a scandal, now dying in a coastal town. Returning to the family he abandoned, Cyrus must confront why they arranged their lives around her silence, and choose between duty to his father's legacy and love for the found family Marisol built. He finally tastes again at her deathbed table, and ends the book by publishing not a review but a letter that renames himself and claims his own identity.
about_author: Ulyana Nystrom is the pen name of a former line cook who spent a decade in kitchens from Lisbon to Oaxaca before turning to fiction. She writes about appetite, memory, and the families we assemble rather than inherit.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. We meet him filing a glowing review of a meal he tasted nothing, living in a beautiful apartment he treats like a hotel room. His editor praises him; he feels like a fraud. Emotional beat: numb competence masking grief.

chapters.title: Static
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Driving home, a radio station plays a song he knows note for note — one his brother Teo wrote the summer before drowning, never recorded. The DJ credits 'M. Reyes.' Cyrus pulls over, shaking. Beat: the past breaks through the present.

chapters.title: What the Family Agreed Not to Say
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, young Cyrus's POV. The Villalobos household the year Teo died: Marisol, Teo's collaborator and lover, blamed for the accident, quietly paid off and exiled by patriarch Aurelio. Everyone signed the silence differently. Beat: how a family builds its architecture of denial.

chapters.title: A Man Who Eats for a Living
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. He investigates M. Reyes through music archives while maintaining his critic persona at a press dinner where he performs enjoyment flawlessly. A young chef, Priya, notices he never actually swallows. Beat: being seen for the first time in years.

chapters.title: The Address on the Postcard
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Among Teo's belongings, kept by their aunt Rosa, he finds unsent postcards addressed to Marisol in a coastal town called Punta Clara. Rosa admits she kept them out of cowardice and gives him all of them. Beat: inheritance of guilt.

chapters.title: Punta Clara
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. He arrives in the faded seaside town and finds Marisol runs a tiny cantina where she cooks but never plays music. He watches her from across the room, unable to approach. Beat: awe and terror of the person his family wronged.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Cooks Without Salt
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She notices the stranger who orders everything and finishes nothing, recognizes the Villalobos jaw immediately, and says nothing — she has known this day might come for thirty years. Beat: guarded hospitality as a test.

chapters.title: First Course
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She serves Cyrus a dish she made for Teo the night he died, watching him eat it. He weeps without tasting it — and confesses he can't taste anything at all. She doesn't forgive him, but she lets him wash dishes. Beat: confession without absolution.

chapters.title: The House That Music Built
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. He meets Marisol's chosen family: her nephew Beto, a deaf drummer who feels rhythm through the floorboards; Luz, a runaway teenager; old Chuy who repairs radios. They are wary of him but fold him into chores. Beat: first glimpse of a family assembled, not inherited.

chapters.title: Duty Calls
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. His father Aurelio, now frail, learns where Cyrus is and demands he come home: the family restaurant's anniversary approaches and Cyrus must write the tribute piece. Cyrus refuses; Aurelio threatens disinheritance. Beat: the old machinery of control grinding back to life.

chapters.title: Beto's Floorboards
chapters.summary: Beto's POV. Beto teaches Cyrus to feel music through vibration, pressing his hands to the drum skin, then to the cantina floor when Marisol finally, privately, plays Teo's song. Cyrus feels it in his chest. Beat: taste and hearing returning through the body.

chapters.title: Luz Runs
chapters.summary: Luz's POV. Luz, terrified of being sent back to her mother, steals the postcards and nearly flees; Cyrus finds her at the bus depot and tells her the truth about his family instead of lecturing her. She comes home. Beat: Cyrus becomes, accidentally, someone's anchor.

chapters.title: The Unfinished Verse
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She reveals the song was never finished because Teo died before writing the last verse — and she has been unable to complete it for thirty years. She asks Cyrus what Teo would have said. Beat: shared authorship of grief begins.

chapters.title: Anniversary
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Under pressure, Cyrus returns briefly to the city, writes the tribute piece praising his father, and hates every word. At the celebration he watches his family perform love for a camera and realizes he has been a tenant there too. Beat: complicity and its cost.

chapters.title: Diagnosis
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol collapses; the doctor gives her months. She tells no one except Chuy, and asks him to keep cooking normal so the family won't grieve early. Beat: dramatic irony tightens — time is running out, as the blurb promised.

chapters.title: Salt
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cooking beside Marisol, Cyrus tastes something — faintly, shockingly: salt. He spits it out and laughs and cries at once. Marisol watches him and finally calls him by his name, not 'the boy.' Beat: resurrection of the senses.

chapters.title: The Question
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus asks the question the whole family arranged itself around: did Teo's death have anything to do with Marisol — or did Aurelio invent her guilt to protect the restaurant's name? Marisol shows him Teo's last letter, hidden decades. Beat: the buried truth surfaces.

chapters.title: Teo's Last Letter
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, Teo's letter in his voice. The letter reveals Teo was leaving the family business for music and Marisol, and that his death was an accident Aurelio twisted into blame. Cyrus reads it aloud to Marisol. Beat: vindication arriving thirty years too late.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Table
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus brings Aurelio to Punta Clara and reads the letter to his face before the whole assembled family. Aurelio does not apologize; he simply ages ten years in a minute. Cyrus chooses the cantina over the legacy. Beat: climax — love against duty, decided.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Marisol and Cyrus's alternating POV. Together they finish Teo's song — Cyrus contributing words, Marisol melody — and perform it once in the cantina with Beto feeling the beat through the floor, Luz singing harmony. Beat: the family made whole by making something together.

chapters.title: Postcards, Finally Sent
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. In her final weeks, Marisol mails Teo's postcards to herself, one per day, reading them aloud at dinner. Her last evening is a long table meal where Cyrus cooks and, for the first time, tastes everything. Beat: grace, mortality, and fullness.

chapters.title: Byline
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus publishes his final column — not a review but a letter resigning from criticism, telling the truth about his family and his tongue, signed with a name he chose for himself. In Punta Clara, the cantina reopens under a new sign: Postcards and Language. Beat: identity claimed; resolution.
